question: A 45 year old bee keeper presents with sudden onset abdominal cramping, dizziness and a swollen tongue. Which of the following statements regarding the management of anaphylaxis is correct?
options: Nebulised adrenaline is first line treatment for bronchospasm in the setting of severe anaphylaxis
There is good quality evidence to support the use of a combination of H1 and H2 antagonists for the management of severe anaphylaxis
Treatment with intravenous steroids is first line for management of severe anaphylaxis
Intravenous Glucagon should be considered in patients who take regular beta blockers who have severe prolonged anaphylaxis refractory to standard first line management
source_notes: A – First line management is IM adrenaline. Nebulised adrenaline for upper airway involvement with stridor or pre-intubation. Nebulised Salbutamol for bronchospasm with addition of magnesium is refractory to initial treatment. B – H1 receptor antagonist is first line for treatment of skin reaction. Addition of an H2 receptor antagonist is possibly more effective than H1 used alone, although evidence is minimal and onset of effect is slow. There is possibly a role for H2 antagonists in severe or refractory anaphylaxis, although evidence is not robust. C – First line management = ABCs, adrenaline, IV fluids. Steroids are of little benefit acutely. Given early in management to prevent prolonged or biphasic reaction. D – Glucagon should be considered for patients who take ß-blockers with severe prolonged anaphylaxis or hypotension refractory to adrenaline & fluids. Adult = 1mg IV every 5 mins, child = 15mcg/kg IV. Glucagon stimulates higher cAMP levels and overrides alpha/beta receptors so that adrenaline does not require those receptor pathways to work. Positive inotrope/chronotrope. Clinical use is based on case reports. Evidence is limited but supports use of glucagon where standard management is not successful. http://emj.bmj.com/content/22/4/272.2
updated_guidance: IM adrenaline is first-line for anaphylaxis. IV glucagon may be considered for refractory hypotension in beta-blocked patients with specialist support; evidence is limited. Steroids/antihistamines are not first-line life-saving therapy.

question: A 40 year old female with a background of severe psoriasis presents to the ED with a dry cough, exertional shortness of breath and fatigue. Which of the following disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug is associated with interstitial pneumonitis?
source_notes: A – Azathioprine complications nausea, stomatitis, bone marrow suppression, rash. Hepatitis & pancreatitis are uncommon. Possible increased risk of lymphoma & skin cancers. B - Methotrexate & Leflunomide can cause lung toxicity. Leflunomide – typically in 1st few months & in combination with Methotrexate. Methotrexate – higher risk of lung toxicity if longer duration of treatment, rheumatoid involvement of lungs/pleura, extra-articular manifestations, DM, age, smoker. Interstitial pneumonitis: This is an uncommon but potentially fatal complication of methotrexate treatment. The risk factors for methotrexate lung are not well understood, but may include pre-existing lung disease or an abnormal chest radiograph. Patients taking methotrexate who present with dry cough, shortness of breath on exertion, malaise, fever and diffuse crackles on auscultation should discontinue taking methotrexate until evaluated further. The chest X-ray may be normal. The differential diagnosis includes Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, and bronchoscopy may be required to exclude this. Corticosteroids are frequently given for methotrexate-induced interstitial pneumonitis. Can require ICU. Mortality is low <1%. C – Cyclosporin complications include renal impairment (acute mediated by renal vasoconstrictions or chronic and cause permanent damage), hypertension, electrolyte disturbance, hyperuricaemia, hirsutism. D – Sulphasalazine complications include nausea, rash (maculo-papular or pruritic), Stevens-Johnsons syndrome, reversible oligospermia. More serios SEs include neutropenia and aplastic anaemia. ** Note in the ASSURE trial (Lancet 2016) compared Abatacept to placebo for RA treatment. There was an increased incidence of respiratory SAEs in Abatecept patients who had history of COPD. Ref: http://www.medsafe.govt.nz/profs/PUarticles/dmards.htm#Aza Cameron 4th edition page 576-577
updated_guidance: Methotrexate can cause pneumonitis; also consider infection (including opportunistic infection) and other pulmonary pathology. Escalate and withhold methotrexate pending specialist assessment if suspected.

question: A 55 year old female who is long term treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus presents to the ED with blurred vision and areas of vision loss noticed when reading. Which of the following disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs is most likely to be the cause?
source_notes: Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Increased risk with higher dose and longer duration of therapy. Renal impairment and concomitant use of Tamoxifen increase risk. In up to 50% of people taking over 20 years. Overall 7.5% of patients taking Hydroxychloroquie for over 5 years may have some retinal damage. Greater risk of toxic retinopathy with Chloroquine than Hydroxychloroquine. Irreversible damage. Asymptomatic in early stages. Patients may report paracentral scotoma, difficulty reading, diminished colour vision. Progresses to loss of acuity, peripheral vision and night vision. On examination – ‘Bull’s eye maculopathy’. In 2016, with new scientific data, the American Academy of Ophthalmology revised the screening recommendations for patients to be commenced on longterm hydroxychloroquine therapy. Fundal examination alone is insufficient for screening, and further tests are required including at least automated visual fields and spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD OCT). Patients with hydroxychloroquine-induced retinal toxicity will not have any visual symptoms in the early stages, and will only develop clinical symptoms with severe endstage damage. Therefore, it is important that the screening recommendations outlined above are followed, and hydroxychloroquine should be ceased if there are signs of definite retinopathy. The retinopathy does not reverse, but progression is rare following cessation of hydroxychloroquine. Visual symptoms may present as paracentral scotomas (islands of vision loss) when reading. Should blurring or vision changes occur, hydroxychloroquine should be ceased and a careful eye examination conducted. Note – eye complications of SLE are uncommon. Can get keratoconjuncitivitis sicca (dry eyes), scelritis, lupus retinopathy (usually in context of acute systemic disease), retinal vasculitis, hypertensive retinopathy, lupus choroidopathy. Ref: https://www.rcophth.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Hydroxychloroquine-and-Chloroquine-Retinopathy-Screening-Guideline-Recommendations.pdf https://www.dermnetnz.org/topics/hydroxychloroquine/
updated_guidance: Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy can be irreversible. Screening uses retinal imaging (e.g. OCT) and functional tests according to local ophthalmology guidance, not fundoscopy alone.

question: A 35 year old female patient presents to ED with a fever, flank pain and dysuria. She reports taking 40mg subcutaneous Adalimumab (Humira) fortnightly for Crohn’s disease, which is now well controlled. Which of the following is true with regards to Adalimumab?
options: Influenza vaccine is contraindicated once therapy has started
Commonly associated with increase in seizures
Can cause fatal reactivation of Hepatitis B in chronic carriers
Common complication is an inflammatory pericarditis
source_notes: TNF alpha inhibitors include Adalimumab (Humira), Etanercept (Enbrel) & Infliximab (Remicade). A – Yearly flu vaccine is recommended. Patients on Humira may receive concurrent vaccines except for live vaccines. No data available on secondary transmission of infection by live vaccines in patient receiving Humira. Ideally paediatric patients should be brought upt to date with imms prior to starting Humira therapy. B – Common neuro complication is headache. Humira has been associated with rare cases of new onset or exacerbation of clinical symptoms of CNS demyelinating diseases such as MS and optic neuritis, and peripheral demyelinating disease including GBS. C – Fatal cases have most often been in patients on multiple immune modulating agents. Absolute CI’s to starting treatment = untreated chronic infection such as Tb, current acute infection, mod-severe CHF, hypersensitivity to murine proteins. Relative CI’s = intercurrent febrile illness, chronic Hep B, hx of GBS/optic neuritis/MS, pregnancy. D – can cause worsening of heart failure with an associated increased in mortality due to CHF. Humira is contraindicated in moderate or severe heart failure. Discontinue treatment if new or worsening symptoms of CHF. Ref: http://medsafe.govt.nz/profs/datasheet/h/humirainjpeninj.pdf
updated_guidance: TNF-alpha inhibitors may reactivate hepatitis B; screen and manage HBV risk before and during therapy. Inactivated influenza vaccination is generally recommended.

question: A 14 year old male patient presents to ED with a fever but seems otherwise well. He reports taking long term Tocilizumab (Actemra) for juvenile idiopathic arthritis, symptoms of which are currently well controlled. Which of the following is true regarding infection in this patient?
options: Patient can safely be discharged with no further investigations or treatment if CRP is normal
Clear chest x-ray absolutely excludes pneumonia
A rash consistent with active varicella zoster is present, it is safe to discharge patient and advise Paracetamol for fever as required
If serious infection suspected, treat infection and postpone next dose of immunosuppressant
source_notes: A – Tocilizumab inhibits IL6 impairing acute-phase response. May completely suppress CRP production even in context of severe sepsis. High index of suspicion of significant infection in this patient group. Ref: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24177456 B – typical xray changes particularly in erly presentation, may be lacking C – Requires discussion with Paeds/Rheum + IV acyclovir. Clear guidelines available regarding whether VZIG is required. Ref: https://www.starship.org.nz/for-health-professionals/starship-clinical-guidelines/i/immunosuppression-infection-and-immunisation-in-rheumatology/
updated_guidance: IL-6 inhibition by tocilizumab can blunt CRP and fever; normal CRP does not exclude serious infection. Suspected serious infection needs prompt assessment and discussion about holding treatment.
